summary: This informational memo updates RFC 1816 and describes registration policies for the .GOV top-level domain, meant to give US federal agencies recognizable names. It aims to avoid name duplication and limit registrations to appropriate agencies.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2146 is the registration policy for the .GOV domain. It says which federal bodies may hold a name directly under .GOV, how that name must be chosen, and how the duplicates and the older registrations are dealt with. Its guiding rule is one agency, one name, so that a visitor who sees a .GOV address can tell which agency runs it.

questions: one agency one name dns policy
subtitle: The Federal Networking Council's rules for who may register a name directly under .GOV: one agency, one name.

tldr.problem: The .GOV domain was filling up with second-level names that did not line up with the actual structure of the US government, so the same agency could hold several names and a visitor could not tell which part of government a site belonged to.
tldr.mechanism: The memo makes eligibility depend on two published lists of federal entities, allows exactly one registration per agency on a first-come first-served basis, derives the name from the agency's official name, and grand-fathers what was registered before August 1995 while setting a deadline of August 1998 to resolve duplicates.
tldr.outcome: The policy also anticipates moving the .GOV registrations into the FED.US domain, and it treats using a domain name to advertise a service as ineffective, so agencies are told to rely on search engines instead.

facts.label: Documents defining eligible entities
facts.value: FIPS 95-1 and the US Government Manual

today: RFC 2146 is an Informational memo published in May 1997, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It provides an update and clarification to RFC 1816 with the registration policy for the .GOV domain, and it anticipates the migration of the .GOV domain into the FED.US domain.

sections.title: Why the .GOV Domain Needs Rules
sections.content:
The .GOV domain is delegated from the root authority to the US Federal Networking Council. It is for registration of US governmental entities on the federal level only, and registrations for state and local governmental agencies are to be made under the .US domain in accordance with that domain's policies. Further references in the document to .GOV should be understood to apply to FED.US as well.

The purpose of the domain is to provide naming conventions that identify US Federal government agencies in order to facilitate access to their electronic resources, and to give guidance for registrations that avoids name duplication and facilitates responsiveness to the public. The policy restricts registrations to coincide with the approved structure of the US government and the advice of its Chief Information Officers. Two documents are recognized as the documentation of that structure: FIPS 95-1, which gives a standard recognized structure into which .GOV and FED.US registrations can fit, and the US Government Manual, a special publication of the Federal Register, which gives official documentation and may be subject to more timely updates. Either document is suitable for deciding which entities qualify. As a side effect the memo says it reduces the number of .GOV and FED.US registrations and the workload on the registration authority.

The most succinct form of the policy is "one agency, one name". The agency may choose its own name, but an easily recognized acronym is suggested. The document also anticipates the migration of the .GOV domain into the FED.US domain, in keeping with common practice on the Internet at the time.
sections.plainLanguage: The domain exists so that people can tell from a web address which federal agency they have reached. The rule that does the work is simple: an agency gets one name, and that name matches the agency's official name in a published government list.

sections.title: Which Entities May Register
sections.content:
FIPS 95-1, "Codes for the Identification of Federal and Federally Assisted Organizations", lists the official names of US Government agencies, and either that document or the US Government Manual can be used to determine whether an entity is eligible for registration as a second-level domain of .GOV. Top-level entities, such as a department in FIPS 95-1 with a code ending in 00, and independent agencies and organizations, such as the National Science Foundation, are eligible to register directly under .GOV. Cross-agency collaborative organizations, such as the Federal Networking Council and the Information Infrastructure Task Force, are eligible upon presentation of the chartering document, and are the only organizations not listed in either document that may register under .GOV.

Several groups are not eligible. Subsidiary, non-autonomous components of a top-level or other entity may not register separately and should register as third-level domains under their parent organization, and international organizations are not eligible at all. Organizations listed as "Federally Aided Organizations" in FIPS 95-1 are not eligible and should register under .ORG or another appropriate top-level domain. Organizations subsidiary to the Department of Defense must register under the .MIL domain through the Defense Data Network Information Center. Any other entity may be registered by request of a cognizant Chief Information Officer, who is the agency official designated by the agency head under the requirements of the Information Technology Management Reform Act of 1996 and Executive Order 13011.

Federal courts constitute a special class of domains. All Federal courts seeking domain registrations should contact the Administrative Office of the US Courts for guidance on policy and naming. The string "SUPREME-COURT" is reserved for the Supreme Court domain, and all other courts and their officers and officials should register in .USCOURTS.GOV. The only standard exceptions are changes to governmental structure due to statutory, regulatory or executive directives not yet reflected in the documentation, for which the requesting agency provides documentation; other requests for exception are referred to the Federal Networking Council.
sections.plainLanguage: A body may hold a name directly under .GOV if it appears in one of the two government lists of agencies, or if it is a joint body that shows its charter. A part of a department, a foreign organisation, or a federally aided organisation may not. Courts have their own rule, and the Department of Defense uses .MIL instead.

sections.title: Naming and One Registration per Agency
sections.content:
A domain name should be derived from the official name for the organization, for example "USDA.GOV" or "AGRICULTURE.GOV", and the registration is listed in the registration database under the official name from FIPS 95-1 or the US Government Manual, or under the name in the chartering document.

Only one registration and delegation is made for the purpose of identifying an agency. The .GOV registration authority provides registrations on a first-come, first-served basis. Which portion of the agency is responsible for managing the domain space under a delegated agency domain is an individual agency matter.

Agencies and entities that had multiple registrations under .GOV could retain them until August 1998, but sub-delegations are permitted only under the one name the agency chooses as its permanent name. As of August 1996 the auxiliary domains become un-delegated and revert to the control of the .GOV owner, and as of 2 August 1997 all registrations in the auxiliary domains must be mirrored in the permanent domain, and those names should be used where possible. At the three year point, in August 1998, all auxiliary domain registrations are deleted. Entities already registered in .GOV but not listed in FIPS 95-1 or the US Government Manual, such as DOE labs and state entities, may retain their registration within the constraint of the single registration rule, and no further non-listed registrations will be made. State and local entities are strongly encouraged to re-register under .US, but this is not mandatory.
sections.plainLanguage: An agency picks one name, taken from its official name, and the registry hands it out to whoever asks first. An agency that had several names keeps them until 1998 but can only create new names under the one it has chosen as permanent.

sections.title: Grandfathering, Duplicates and FED.US
sections.content:
The clarification section says that registrations prior to August 1995 are grand-fathered and do not require re-registration, with one exception: duplicate registrations for the same organization at the same level. Two registrations that represent the Department of Transportation would be considered duplicates, while registrations for the Department of Transportation and for the Federal Aviation Administration would not, since the FAA is an autonomous component contained within the DOT. The policy requires resolution of all duplicate registrations by August 1998. Local and state agencies registered under .GOV may remain there, but are strongly encouraged to transfer to the .US domain, and cross-agency collaborative efforts may register under FED.US as an alternative to asking for an exception to the .GOV policy.

The questions and answers show how the policy applies in practice. In August 1995 fewer than half a dozen duplicate DNS names at the FIPS 95-1 level needed to be changed, so over three years the cost was expected to be minimal. Departments with duplicate names, such as STATE.GOV and LABOR.GOV, had six months, until December 1996, to determine which name was permanent and which auxiliary, and three years to drop the auxiliary registration. Agencies such as the CDC, NIST, NIH and FDA, which are not listed in FIPS 95-1, keep their existing names, because the policy only governs the domains allowed to be registered directly under .GOV and further delegations are under the control of the subdomain owner.

For future registrations, the registrar uses the memo as guidance and will not grant .GOV to any new entity that is not listed in FIPS 95-1 or the US Government Manual, or that has not been granted exception status by the Federal Networking Council Executive Committee. The memo also explains the intent: to avoid confusion as more entities register under .GOV, and to transfer authority and responsibility for the domain name space to the appropriate agencies and away from a centralized authority.
sections.plainLanguage: What was registered before August 1995 stays, except where one agency holds two names for itself, which had to be sorted out by August 1998. Agencies not on the government lists keep their names too, and new registrants are turned away unless they are listed or have been given an exception.

sections.title: Practical Questions from Agencies
sections.content:
On DNS resolution, the answer is that it depends on how servers are configured. Most servers cache previous answers, information directly under .GOV will be fairly long-lived which reduces the requirement to query the .GOV server, and multiple levels of the DNS tree may reside on the same server, so the information for DHHS.GOV, PHS.DHHS.GOV and CDC.PHS.DHHS.GOV could all sit on one server. Assuming the location of the DHHS.GOV server was not cached, that would take two queries, and later queries would be served from the cache.

On using domain names for advertising a service, the memo is discouraging. It says there is no empirical data showing that domain names are effective for that, and that a user with freely available search engines could locate the information before successfully guessing the domain name. If an agency CIO deems it advisable to advertise by domain name anyway, the agency should use the WHOIS utility to determine whether similar or conflicting names exist in domains such as .COM and .ORG, since any advertising value may be lost if the same or a similar name exists in more than one domain. An agency that finds its name already used in .COM and .ORG is told that the only practical way to prevent confusing customers is to register the name in all available domains and hold them, without using them, so the site cannot be spoofed. Using domains other than .GOV or FED.US is a policy matter under the statutory authorities of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs of the Office of Management and Budget, so agency CIOs are advised to consult OMB first.

An agency that would rather have a third-level domain but whose parent has no second-level domain, or does not provide third-level registration services, should contact the official administrative contact for the second-level domain, found with the whois command. The domain administrators have the responsibility of providing third-level registration services. If an exception is granted because there is no appropriate second-level domain, it is valid for only two years after the subsequent establishment of an appropriate domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the memo is questions from agencies that were worried about the policy. The answers are practical: deeper names do not slow the DNS down, using a domain name to advertise a service is not effective, and an agency that wants a name under a parent it does not have should contact that parent's administrator.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says the integrity of the information in the DNS databases, made available through network protocols, is not reliable in the Internet environment without additional cryptographic controls or secure lines. Agencies with secure internal network lines may be able to count on their internal naming information as accurate, but users on the Internet cannot. The DNS system may be enhanced by the use of digital signatures on the information provided, and as this software becomes available, .GOV second-level domain administrators are encouraged to use it to provide a secure binding for the information associated with DNS names.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo warns that a DNS answer can be changed in transit, so the names in the .GOV zone cannot be trusted over the public Internet unless they are signed. It asks the administrators of those zones to start using digital signatures as the software appears.

viz.caption: THE PRACTICAL QUESTIONS AGENCIES ASKED, AND THE MEMO'S ANSWERS

items.title: Does a deeper name slow the DNS down?
items.text: No. Servers cache answers, and several levels of the tree can sit on one server.

items.title: Should a domain name advertise a service?
items.text: The memo discourages it: there is no evidence it works, and a search engine may find the service first.

items.title: What if the same name exists in .COM?
items.text: Register it in the other domains and hold it, so customers are not confused and the site cannot be spoofed.

items.title: What if my parent has no second-level domain?
items.text: The registration authority supplies contact information or grants an exception, valid for two years.
